cues.text: ODYSSEY — BOOK XV
Telemachus called home;\nTheoclymenus; the life of Eumaeus.
But Pallas Athena went her way to\nwide-dancing-grounded Lacedaemon
to remind the shining son of great-hearted Odysseus\nof his homecoming, and to stir him to return.
She found Telemachus and Nestor's splendid son\nsleeping in the forecourt of glorious Menelaus —
Nestor's son, at least, mastered by soft sleep;
but no sweet sleep held Telemachus: through the ambrosial\nnight cares for his father kept his heart awake.
And gray-eyed Athena stood near him and spoke:
"Telemachus, it is no longer good,\nthis roaming far from home
with your goods abandoned, and men in your own house
of such overbearing insolence —\nor they will devour it all,
dividing your goods among them,\nand your journey come to nothing.
Rouse Menelaus of the great war-cry — quickly —
to send you off, so you may find\nyour blameless mother still at home.
For already her father and her brothers press her\nto marry Eurymachus: he outbids all the suitors
in gifts, and keeps raising the bride-price higher.
Take care nothing is carried\nfrom the house against your will.
You know what kind of heart is in a woman's breast:
she wants to swell the house of the man who marries her,
and of her former children,\nof the wedded husband she has lost,
she thinks no more once he is dead. She asks nothing.
No — go back yourself and put everything in the hands\nof whichever of the slave-women seems the best to you,
until the gods reveal to you your honored bride.
And another word I will tell you: lay it up in your heart.
The best men of the suitors lie\nin wait for you — deliberately —
in the strait between Ithaca and rugged Samos,\nhungry to kill you before you reach your fathers' land.
But I do not look for that. No:\nsooner will the earth close over
more than one of the suitor-men who eat away your living.
Keep your well-made ship far out from the islands,
and sail by night as well as day:\nthat one of the deathless ones
who guards and keeps you will send a breeze behind you.
And when you reach the first shore of Ithaca,\nsend the ship and all the companions on to the city,
but yourself, before all else, go to the swineherd
who keeps your swine —\nwhose heart is loyal to you all the same.
Sleep the night there; and send him into the city\nto carry the news to watchful-minded Penelope:
that you are safe, and have come home from Pylos."
So speaking, she went away to high Olympus.
And he woke Nestor's son out of his sweet sleep,\nrousing him with a kick of his heel, and said to him:
"Wake up, Peisistratus, son of Nestor.\nBring out the strong-hoofed
horses and yoke them under the chariot,\nso we can be on our road."
Then Peisistratus, Nestor's son, answered him:
"Telemachus — however we press for the road, there is no
driving through the pitch-dark night.\nAnd it will soon be dawn.
Wait, then, until the hero Atreus' son, Menelaus
famed for the spear, brings his\ngifts and sets them in the chariot
and sends us on our way with kindly words.
For a guest remembers, all his days,\nthe host who shows him kindness."
So he spoke; and at once Dawn\nof the golden throne came on.
And Menelaus of the great war-cry came up to them,\nfresh-risen from his bed, from beside fair-haired Helen.
When the dear son of Odysseus caught sight of him,\nhe hurried the shining tunic on about his body
and threw his great mantle over his sturdy shoulders —
the young hero — and went out; and coming up beside him,\nTelemachus, dear son of godlike Odysseus, said:
"Menelaus, son of Atreus,\nZeus-nurtured, leader of peoples:
send me back now, at last, to my own dear fatherland,\nfor now my heart is longing to go home."
Then Menelaus of the great war-cry answered him:
"Telemachus — far be it from me to hold you here for long,
when you strain for home. I would blame another man\nas much for it — a host who loved beyond measure
or hated beyond measure:\ndue measure is better in all things.
It is equal wrong to push out a guest who does\nnot wish to go, and to hold one back who is eager.
Cherish the guest who is with you;\nspeed the one who would leave.
Only wait until I bring my gifts\nand set them in the chariot —
beautiful gifts; your own eyes will\nsee them — and I tell the women
to lay a meal in the hall from the plenty stored within.
It is both honors at once — the glory and the profit —
to dine before you go, over the wide and boundless earth.
And if you care to swing through\nHellas and the heart of Argos,
I will go with you myself: I will yoke you horses
and guide you through the cities\nof men; and no one will send us
away as we came — each will give\nus one thing at least to carry:
some tripod of fine bronze, or a cauldron,\nor a pair of mules, or a golden cup."
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered him:
"Menelaus, son of Atreus,\nZeus-nurtured, leader of peoples,
I want to go home to our own place now. For when I\nleft I set no guard behind me over my possessions:
I fear I may perish myself, hunting my godlike father,\nor some fine treasure vanish from my halls."
And when Menelaus of the great war-cry heard it,\nat once he told his wife and her slave-women
to lay a meal in the hall from the plenty stored within.
And Eteoneus, Boethous' son, came up to him,\njust out of bed — for he lived not far away —
and Menelaus of the great war-cry bade him light the fire
and roast some of the meat. He heard, and did not disobey.
And Menelaus himself went down to\nhis fragrant treasure-chamber —
not alone: Helen went with him, and Megapenthes.
And when they came to where his treasures lay,\nAtreus' son took up a two-handled cup,
and bade his son Megapenthes carry the mixing-bowl\nof silver; and Helen stood by the chests
where her robes lay, worked all over\nwith figures — she had made them herself.
Helen lifted one of them out, shining among women:
the one loveliest in its weaving, and the amplest,\nglittering like a star; it lay lowest of all the rest.
Then they went back up through\nthe house until they reached
Telemachus; and fair-haired Menelaus said to him:
"Telemachus — your homecoming, as your heart desires it,
may Zeus accomplish, the loud-thundering lord of Hera.
Of all the treasures lying stored in my house I\nwill give you the most beautiful, the most honored:
I will give you a wrought mixing-bowl —\nall silver it is, and its rims are finished off in gold —
the work of Hephaestus. The hero Phaedimus gave it,\nking of the Sidonians, when his house sheltered me
on my way home there. This I would send with you."
So speaking, the hero Atreus' son set the two-handled\ncup in his hands; and strong Megapenthes carried in
the shining mixing-bowl of silver and set it before him;\nand Helen of the lovely cheeks stood by
with the robe in her hands,\nand spoke a word, and named him:
"I too have a gift for you, dear child — this:
a keepsake of Helen's hands,\nagainst the hour of the marriage
you long for, for your bride\nto wear. Until then let it lie
in your dear mother's keeping. And may you come rejoicing\nto your well-built house and your own fatherland."
So speaking she set it in his hands;\nand he received it gladly.
And the hero Peisistratus took the gifts and stowed them
in the chariot-basket, wondering at them all in his heart.
Then fair-haired Menelaus led them into the house,\nand the two of them sat down on benches and high seats.
A handmaid brought water for their hands in a pitcher,
a beautiful golden one, and poured it over a silver basin
for them to wash, and drew up\na polished table beside them.
The grave housekeeper brought\nbread and set it before them,
laying out delicacies in plenty,\ngiving gladly of her store;
and close by, Boethous' son carved\nthe meat and shared the portions,
and the son of glorious Menelaus poured the wine.
And their hands went out to the\ngood things spread before them.
But when they had put away desire for food and drink,\nthen Telemachus and Nestor's splendid son
yoked the horses and mounted the inlaid chariot\nand drove out of the gateway and the echoing porch.
And after them came Atreus' son, fair-haired Menelaus,\nbearing honey-hearted wine in his right hand,
in a golden cup, for them to pour before they went.
He stood before the horses, and pledging them he spoke:
"Farewell, young men — and carry my greeting to Nestor,
shepherd of the people:\ntruly he was gentle as a father to me
while we sons of the Achaeans made war at Troy."
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered him:
"All this, Zeus-nurtured, just as you say, we will\ntell him when we come. And would that I as surely,
arriving home in Ithaca, might find Odysseus in the house,
and tell him how I came from you, having met with every\nkindness, and bring home treasures many and fine."
And even as he spoke, a bird flew by on the right hand:
an eagle, carrying in its talons a huge white goose,\na tame one, out of the yard; and men and women
streamed after it, shouting.\nAnd the eagle, closing near them,
shot off to the right,\nin front of the horses. At the sight
their hearts lifted: the spirit warmed in every breast,\nand among them Peisistratus, Nestor's son, began:
"Read it, Menelaus, Zeus-nurtured, leader of peoples:
is it for us two the god has\nshown this sign, or for yourself?"
So he spoke; and Menelaus, dear to Ares,\npondered how he might read it rightly and reply.
But long-robed Helen was before him, and spoke out:
"Hear me — and I will prophesy as the immortals cast\nit in my heart, and as I think it will be accomplished.
As this eagle snatched the goose fattened in the house,
coming out of the mountain where\nhis kin are, and his birthplace,
so Odysseus, after much suffering and much wandering,
will come home and take his vengeance — or even now he\nis home already, planting evil for all the suitors."
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered her:
"May Zeus grant it so, the loud-thundering lord of Hera:
then even there I would pray to you as to a god."
He spoke, and laid the whip to the\nhorses; and they, full of fire,
sprang quickly through the city toward the plain.
All day long they shook the yoke they bore between them.
The sun went down, and all the ways grew dark,\nand they came to Pherae, to the house of Diocles,
son of Ortilochus, whom Alpheus fathered.
There they slept the night,\nand he set guest-gifts before them.
When Dawn appeared, the early-born, with fingers of rose,
they yoked the horses and mounted the inlaid chariot\nand drove out of the gateway and the echoing porch;
and he whipped them to a run,\nand the pair flew on, nothing loath.
And soon they came to the steep citadel of Pylos.
Then Telemachus spoke to the son of Nestor:
"Son of Nestor — will you\nundertake a thing for me and see it
done, as I ask? Guest-friends\nfrom of old we may call ourselves,
from our fathers' friendship —\nand we are of one age besides,
and this journey has set us still more of one mind.
Do not drive me past my ship,\nZeus-nurtured: leave me there —
where the old man will keep me in his house against my will,\naching to host me. And I must get home quickly."
So he spoke; and Nestor's son debated with his heart\nhow he might undertake it rightly, and see it done.
And as he weighed it, this seemed to him the better way:
he turned the horses toward the\nfast ship and the shore of the sea,
and in the ship's stern he unloaded the beautiful gifts,\nthe clothing and the gold that Menelaus gave;
and urging Telemachus on, he spoke winged words to him:
"Aboard with you now — quick —\nand order all your companions,
before I reach home and bring the old man the news.
For I know this well, in my mind and in my heart:
so overpowering is his spirit, he will not let you go —
he will come down here himself\nto summon you, and I tell you
he will not go back empty-handed.\nAngry he will be, whatever happens."
So speaking he drove the fine-maned horses back to the\ncity of the Pylians, and quickly reached the house.
And Telemachus called to his\ncompanions and commanded them:
"Set the tackle in order,\ncompanions, through the black ship,
and let us board ourselves, and be on our road."
So he spoke, and they listened well and obeyed:
and they came aboard at once and\ntook their places at the oarlocks.
So he busied himself;\nand by the stern of the ship he prayed
and sacrificed to Athena.\nAnd there came up beside him a man
from a far country, in flight from Argos for\nkilling a man — a seer, of the lineage of Melampus,
who once, in time past, lived in Pylos mother of flocks,
a rich man among the Pylians, in a house of great wealth;
but he fled to another people, away from his fatherland
and from great-hearted Neleus, proudest of living men,\nwho held his vast estate by force a full year round;
while Melampus, all that time, in the halls of Phylacus\nlay bound in bitter bonds, suffering strong pains
for the sake of Neleus' daughter,\nand the deep blindness of heart
that the goddess laid on him,\nthe Fury who strikes the house.
Yet he escaped his doom, and drove the deep-lowing\ncattle from Phylace to Pylos, and paid the ugly deed
of godlike Neleus back, and led the woman home
to be his brother's wife.\nAnd he himself went to another people,
to horse-pasturing Argos: there it was fated for\nhim to live from then on, ruling over many Argives.
There he married a wife and built a high-roofed house,
and fathered Antiphates and Mantius, strong sons both.
Antiphates fathered great-hearted Oicles,\nand Oicles Amphiaraus, the rouser of armies,
whom Zeus who bears the aegis and Apollo loved
in their hearts, with every kind\nof love; yet he never reached
the threshold of old age:\nhe died at Thebes — a woman's bribes.
And to him were born sons, Alcmaeon and Amphilochus.
And Mantius, in his turn, fathered Polypheides and Cleitus —\nbut Cleitus golden-throned Dawn snatched away,
for his beauty's sake, to live among the immortals;\nand of high-hearted Polypheides Apollo made a seer
far the best among mortals, once Amphiaraus was dead.
He moved to Hyperesia, angry at his father,\nand dwelling there he prophesied for all men.
It was this man's son who now came up —\nTheoclymenus was his name — and stood beside Telemachus.
He found him pouring wine and praying by his fast
black ship, and he raised his\nvoice and spoke winged words:
"Friend — since I find you\nburning offerings in this place,
I beg you by these offerings, and by the god, and then
by your own head, and your companions' who go with you:
tell me truly what I ask; hold nothing back.
What man are you, and from where?\nWhere are your city and your parents?"
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered him:
"Then I will tell you, stranger, and tell you truly.
By birth I am of Ithaca; my father is Odysseus —\nif he ever was; by now he has died some grim death.
That is why I took companions and a black ship\nand came out for news of my father, so long gone."
Then godlike Theoclymenus said to him:
"So I too am out of my country: I killed a man of\nmy own tribe; and his brothers and kinsmen are many
in horse-pasturing Argos,\nwith great power among the Achaeans.
It is their death I flee — the black doom of their\nhands — since now it is my lot to wander among men.
Take me aboard your ship,\nsince in my flight I have found you
begging: or they will kill me.\nI think they are on my track."
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered him:
"Then I will not push you,\nwilling as you are, from the trim ship.
Come with us: there you will be\nmade welcome from what we have."
So he spoke, and took the man's bronze spear from him\nand laid it flat along the deck of the curved ship;
and he himself stepped aboard the seagoing\nvessel and sat down in the stern, and beside him
he seated Theoclymenus.\nAnd his men cast off the stern-lines.
And Telemachus called to his companions and commanded them
to lay hands on the tackle; and they obeyed him swiftly:
they raised the fir mast and stepped it in the\nhollow mast-box, made it fast with the forestays,
and hauled the white sail up by\nthe twisted ox-hide halyards.
And gray-eyed Athena sent them a following wind rushing\nhard through the clear sky, so the ship might run
her course at speed across the salt water of the sea.
And they ran past Crouni,\nand Chalcis of the lovely streams.
The sun went down, and all the ways grew dark,\nand the ship bore on for Pheae, driven by the wind of Zeus,
and along bright Elis, where the Epeians hold power.
From there again he steered her for the Sharp Islands,
wondering whether he would slip past death, or be taken.
And in the hut, meanwhile,\nOdysseus and the noble swineherd
were at supper; and the other\nmen were at supper with them.
When they had put away desire for food and drink,\nOdysseus spoke among them, making trial of the swineherd —
whether he would still befriend\nhim with all care and press him
to stay there at the farmstead,\nor start him toward the city:
"Hear me now, Eumaeus, and all you other companions.
At dawn I want to go off to the city and beg there,\nso as not to wear you down — you and your men.
Only advise me well, and send along a good guide
to bring me there. And through\nthe town I will drift on my own —
I must — and hope someone will hand me a cup and a crust.
And I would come to the house of godlike Odysseus\nand give my news to watchful-minded Penelope,
and mix with those suitors in their insolence —\nthey might spare me a dinner out of their endless plenty.
I would serve well among them, whatever they wanted done.
For I will tell you this — take it in, and hear me out:
by the favor of Hermes the guide, who lends the\ngrace and glory to all the labor of men's hands,
no other mortal can compete with me at service:
at building up a fire, at splitting seasoned wood,\nat carving and at roasting meat, at pouring wine —
all that lesser men do, waiting on the great."
Then, greatly stirred,\nyou answered him, Eumaeus the swineherd:
"Ah, stranger — why has such a thought come into\nyour mind? You must be hungry to die on the spot,
if you truly mean to walk into that crowd of suitors,\nwhose arrogance and violence reach the iron sky.
Their serving-men are nothing like you:
they are young, well-dressed in cloaks and tunics,\nsleek their heads always, and handsome their faces —
those are the men who wait upon the suitors' polished\ntables, loaded down with bread and meat and wine.
No — stay. Nobody is put out by your being here,\nnot I, and not any of my companions with me.
But when the dear son of Odysseus comes,\nthat man will clothe you in a cloak and a tunic,
and send you wherever your heart and spirit bid you go."
Then much-enduring noble Odysseus answered him:
"Eumaeus — may you be as dear to father Zeus
as you are to me: for you have stopped\nmy wandering and my grim misery.
Nothing is more wretched for mortal men than roaming:
it is for the cursed belly's sake men take hard pains,
when wandering and sorrow and grief have come upon them.
But now, since you hold me here to wait for that young man,\ncome, tell me of godlike Odysseus' mother,
and his father, whom he left on the doorsill of old age:
are they still living, somewhere under the rays of the sun,\nor dead by now, and down in the house of Hades?"
Then the swineherd answered him, a leader of men:
"Then I will tell you, stranger, and tell you truly.
Laertes is living still, but praying always
to Zeus that the life may waste\nout of his limbs in his own halls:
so terribly he mourns for his son who is gone,\nand for the wise wife of his youth — her death above all
has broken him, and brought him\nraw old age before his time.
And she died of grief for her son, for her famous son —\na wretched death. May no one die so who lives here
and is a friend to me, and has dealt with me in kindness.
While she still lived, for all her endless sorrow,\nit was some pleasure to me to ask for her and after her,
because she reared me herself, with long-robed Ctimene,\nher stately daughter, the youngest child she bore.
With her I was raised, and honored little less.
But when the two of us came to the threshold of our prime,
they gave her in marriage to Same —\nand got a fortune for her —
while me the lady dressed in a mantle and tunic,\nfine clothes, and bound good sandals on my feet,
and sent me to the farm. But she\nloved me from the heart still more.
Now I go without all that. And yet the blessed gods\nmake the work prosper under my hand, the work I keep to:
from it I have eaten and drunk,\nand given to those I owe respect.
But from the mistress herself\nthere is nothing sweet to hear,
no word, no kindness,\nsince that evil fell upon the house —
those overweening men. And slaves miss it greatly,\nspeaking before the mistress, and learning all the news,
and eating and drinking, and carrying something afterward
off to the fields — the things that warm a slave's heart."
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered him:
"Well — how small you must have been, swineherd Eumaeus,
when you were carried so far from\nyour country and your parents.
But come, tell me this, and tell it to me truly:
was it a wide-wayed city of men that was sacked,\nthe one where your father and your honored mother lived,
or were you alone with your sheep or with your cattle
when raiders took you into\ntheir ships and carried you over
to this man's house, and he paid a worthy price?"
Then the swineherd answered him, a leader of men:
"Stranger, since you ask me this, and want it all —\nlisten in silence now, and take your ease, and sit
drinking your wine. These nights go on past telling.
There is time enough for sleep,\nand time to take joy in listening;
no need to bed down before the hour:\neven sleep grows a weariness.
As for the rest of you —\nwhoever's heart and spirit bid him,
go out and sleep; and at the showing of the dawn eat,\nand follow out the swine of our master.
But we two in the hut, over our drink and food,\nwill take our pleasure in each other's grim sorrows,
remembering them. For afterward a\nman finds pleasure even in pains,
when he has suffered much and wandered far.
So I will tell you what you ask me, what you probe for.
There is an island called Syrie —\nyou may have heard of it —
above Ortygia, where the turnings of the sun are:
not so crowded with people, but a good land,\nrich in herds, rich in flocks, full of wine, deep in wheat.
Famine never enters that country, nor does any\nhateful sickness fall on wretched mortals there:
but when the generations of men grow old in the town,\nApollo of the silver bow comes with Artemis
and visits them with his gentle arrows, and kills them.
and everything is halved between them,\nand over both of them my father was the king —
Ctesius, son of Ormenus, a match for the immortals.
There Phoenicians came — men famed for ships, gnawers,\nwith countless trinkets in their black vessel.
Now in my father's house there was a Phoenician woman,\nbeautiful and tall, and skilled in glorious handwork;
and the Phoenicians, subtle-minded, led her astray.
Washing clothes by the hollow ship, one of them first\nlay with her in love — the thing that leads astray
the minds of women, even one whose works are honest.
Then he asked her who she was, and where she came from,
and she pointed at once to my father's high-roofed house:
'I claim my birth from Sidon, rich in bronze,\nand I am the daughter of Arybas, a man of flowing wealth.
But Taphian pirates snatched me as I came in from\nthe fields, and carried me over the sea and sold me
to this man's house; and he paid a worthy price.'
Then the man who had lain with her in secret said:
'Then would you come home again with us, to look on
the high-roofed house of your\nfather and mother — and on them?
For they are living still, and are called wealthy.'
Then the woman answered him and said:
'Even that could be, if you sailors were willing to\nbind yourselves by oath to bring me home unharmed.'
So she spoke, and they all swore the oath she demanded.
And when they had sworn and sealed the oath entire,\nthe woman spoke among them again and answered:
'Silence, now. Let none of your company say a word\nto me, meeting me in the street or at the well,
or someone may go to the house and tell the old man;\nand he, suspecting, would bind me in hard bonds,
and set his mind on death for all of you.
Keep the word in your hearts,\nand press the buying of your cargo.
But when your ship is full and freighted with goods,\nlet a message come quickly to me at the house.
For I will bring gold too — whatever comes under my hand.
And there is another thing I\nwould gladly give for my passage:
I nurse a child of this fine man in the halls —\nsuch a knowing little thing, always running out beside me.
I would bring him aboard the ship, and he would fetch you
a boundless price, wherever you\nsell him among strange-tongued men.'
So speaking, she went off to the beautiful house.
And they stayed among us a whole year long,\nand bought and gathered goods in their hollow ship;
When the hollow hull was freighted for their crossing,\nthey sent a messenger up to bring the woman word.
A man came, deep in cunning, to my father's house with\na necklace of gold, strung here and there with amber.
And in the hall the slave-women and my honored mother
kept turning it in their hands\nand drinking it with their eyes,
offering him their price;\nand he nodded to the woman in silence.
He nodded — then went his way to the hollow ship;
and she took me by the hand and\nled me out through the doors.
In the forecourt she found the cups and the tables\nof the banqueters, the men who attended on my father:
they had gone out to the people's session and debate.
Quickly she hid three goblets away at her breast
and carried them off. And I followed —\nin my child's witlessness.
The sun went down, and all the ways grew dark,\nand we came at a run to the famous harbor,
where the sea-swift ship of the Phoenician men was lying.
Then they embarked, and went\ntheir way over the watery paths,
with the two of us aboard; and Zeus sent down a wind.
Six days we sailed on, alike by day and night;\nbut when Zeus, the son of Cronos, brought the seventh day,
then Artemis the shooter of arrows struck the woman,
and she dropped with a thud\ninto the bilge, like a sea-tern.
spoil for the seals and fishes,\nand I was left alone, my heart aching.
Then wind and water carried them along to Ithaca,\nand there Laertes bought me, with his own possessions.
So it was my eyes first looked upon this land."
Then Odysseus, seed of Zeus, answered him with words:
"Eumaeus, you have deeply stirred\nthe heart here in my breast,
telling all these things —\nthe sorrows your heart has suffered.
And yet, I say, Zeus set the good beside the evil for you,
since after all that pain you came to the house of a kind
man, who provides your food and drink with every care,\nand you live a good life — while I come to you here
as I am: still wandering through the many cities of men."
So they spoke to each other of such things,\nthen lay down to sleep — no long time, a little only,
for soon Dawn came on her fair throne. And on the\nshore the companions of Telemachus were striking sail:
they took the mast down smartly\nand rowed her in to anchorage,
and threw the mooring-stones out,\nand made the stern-lines fast;
and they themselves stepped out into the breaking\nsurf and readied a meal, and mixed the sparkling wine.
And when they had put away desire for food and drink,\nclear-headed Telemachus began and spoke among them:
"Row the black ship on now, all of you, to the city.
I will make my way to the fields and to the herdsmen,
and at evening, once I have looked\nover the farmlands, I will come down.
In the morning I will set before\nyou the wages of the voyage:
a good feast of meats, and honey-hearted wine."
Then godlike Theoclymenus said to him:
"And where shall I go, dear child? Whose house shall\nI come to, of the men who hold power in rocky Ithaca?
Straight to your mother's house —\nis that where I go — and yours?"
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered him:
"At any other time I would tell you: come to our house —
there is no lack there of what a\nguest is given. But for you, now,
it would be the worse way: I will be gone, and my mother
will not see you. For not often\nbefore the suitors in that house
does she appear: apart from them\nshe weaves at her loom, upstairs.
But I will name you another man you might go to:
Eurymachus, glorious son of thoughtful Polybus,\nwhom now the men of Ithaca look on like a god.
For he is far the best man there — and hungriest of all
to marry my mother and take the honor that was Odysseus'.
But Zeus the Olympian, who has his home in the bright sky,
knows whether before any wedding\nhe will bring their evil day."
And even as he spoke, a bird flew by on his right hand:
a hawk, the swift messenger of Apollo. In its talons
it held a dove, and was tearing it,\nand shook the feathers down
to the ground, midway between\nthe ship and Telemachus himself.
And Theoclymenus called him apart from his companions,
and pressed his hand, and spoke a word, and named him:
"Telemachus, not without a god did\nthat bird fly past on the right:
I knew it, looking at it face-on, for a bird of omen.
There is no line more kingly than your own in the\nland of Ithaca. No: yours is the power forever."
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered him:
"Ah, stranger, if only that word might be accomplished:
then you would quickly know my friendship, and gifts
and plenty for me — any man who\nmet you would call you blessed."
And he turned and spoke to Piraeus, his trusted companion:
"Piraeus, son of Clytius — you who in other things obey me
most of all the companions who followed me to Pylos:
now too, I ask you, take this stranger to your house\nand care for him kindly, and honor him, until I come."
Then Piraeus, famous for the spear, answered him:
"Telemachus, even if you should\nstay out there a long while,
I will look after this man; no guest's due shall he lack."
So speaking, he went aboard the ship,\nand called the companions
to come aboard themselves and loose the stern-lines;
and they came aboard at once and\ntook their places at the oarlocks.
And Telemachus bound his beautiful sandals under his feet
and took his strong spear up from the deck of the ship,
sharp-tipped with bronze.\nAnd the men cast off the stern-lines:
they shoved out and sailed on to the city, as they were\nordered by Telemachus, dear son of godlike Odysseus.
But his feet carried him swiftly,\nstriding, until he reached the yard
where his swine past counting were;\nand beside them the swineherd
slept, a good man, whose heart was loyal to his masters.
